back: $s=(u-\ell)/(2^b-1)$, zero point $z=\operatorname{round}(-\ell/s)$, $q=\operatorname{round}(x/s)+z$, $\hat x=s(q-z)$. Range must include 0.
So that real zero (padding, ReLU outputs, masks) is represented exactly: x=0 gives q=z and dequantises to 0.
$|\hat x-x|\le s/2$ for unclipped values; roughly uniform error gives MSE $\approx s^2/12$.
The scale doubles, so the MSE is multiplied by about 4.
Per-tensor: one scale, set by the largest weight. Per-channel: one scale per output row, so an outlier only damages its own row. Cost: one scale stored per row.

front: What is an outlier in quantisation?
back: A value far larger than the rest; it forces a large scale and coarse resolution for all other values sharing that scale.
Most robust to least: weights, activations (outliers), KV cache (errors accumulate), attention logits (softmax amplifies; keep in 16-bit).
Post-training quantisation rounds a trained model (fast, cheap). Quantisation-aware training simulates rounding during training.
A cheap draft model proposes N tokens; the target verifies all in one parallel pass and keeps a prefix; output law equals the target's.
Accept draft token d with probability $\min(1,q(d)/p(d))$.
On rejection sample from $\max(0,q-p)$ normalised. Its normaliser is $1-\alpha$.

front: Expected tokens per round and speed-up
back: $\mathbb{E}=\frac{1-\alpha^{N+1}}{1-\alpha}$; with draft cost c per token, speed-up $\approx \mathbb{E}/(Nc+1)$ (assumes i.i.d. acceptance).

front: Mixture of experts: what is saved?
back: Compute per token (only top-k experts run), not memory: all experts must be stored. Load balancing keeps experts evenly used.
